ta-l1d34q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 34. Lombard compares person and essence, first by identity, setting out the error that the essence that is the Father is not the Son and its proofs by reason and from Hilary, which he answers by interpreting the authority with attention to Scripture's context (confirmed by Augustine and Hilary) and by granting some distinction of understanding; then by the commonness of the essence to the persons, as essence and as the other attributes, with the reason for appropriation and the meaning of 'homoousion'. He ends the treatise on the Trinity with metaphorical names and an admission of insufficiency before the mystery. Thomas asks three questions: on the comparison of essence and person, on the appropriation in the text, and on what is said of God metaphorically. On the first, whether the essence is the person and whether the three persons can be said to be of one essence.
claims: Person and essence are identical; the essence is common to the persons.
The treatise on the Trinity closes with metaphorical names.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e143.summary: First argument that person and essence are not the same in God. Every divine person begets, is begotten, or proceeds, and the essence does none of these (Dist. 5).
claims: The essence does not beget.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e146.summary: Second argument. Affirmation and negation are never true of the same, but they are of essence and person: the essence is not distinct, the person is.
claims: Contradictory predicates show non-identity.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e149.summary: Third argument. Every person is the supposit of some nature, and nothing can be supposit of itself.
claims: Nothing is its own supposit.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e153.summary: Fourth argument. The proper adds to the common, and the essence is common and the person proper, so the person adds to the essence.
claims: Proper adds to common.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e156.summary: Fifth argument. No two things are united in what is wholly the same as each, since then they could not be distinguished, and Father and Son are united in the essence.
claims: Union in the wholly identical leaves no distinction.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e159.summary: Sed contra from Boethius: in God that by which it is and what is are the same, and essence is signified as that by which, person as what is.
claims: Quo est and quod est are the same in God.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e162.summary: Second sed contra. If the Father's person is not the deity by which he is called God, he is God by participation in a nature, and what is participated is greater than the participant in that respect (Dist. 22; Dionysius), so the deity would be greater than the Father.
claims: Otherwise the Father would be God by participation.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e165.summary: Third sed contra. If the essence were a thing other than the three persons, there would be four things in God, which is heretical.
claims: A distinct essence would make a quaternity.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e168.summary: Thomas's determination. Person and essence are in no way really distinct in God. Where essence differs from hypostasis or supposit there must be something material by which the common nature is individuated and determined to this singular, which the hypostasis adds to the essence in creatures. In God the nature does not subsist through something determining it like matter but subsists by itself and is its own subsistent being, so the nature is what subsists and the being in which it subsists, and in God that by which and what is are entirely the same. So essence and person must be really identical, even if the properties were not the essence, since persons are persons not by underlying properties but by underlying the essence, a person being an individual subsisting in the genus of substance; so a real difference between essence and person would be even more unfitting than between essence and property. Yet they are conceptually distinct, with the truth of the thing as foundation. Since God has supreme simplicity and perfection, we signify him by abstract names for simplicity and concrete names, signifying a subsistent, for perfection; and in God there is something common in reality and something proper. So 'person' signifies God as subsistent and as proper; 'essence' signifies him simply, not as subsistent, and as common; 'paternity' not as subsistent but as proper, as distinguishing, not distinguished. So the person differs from essence and property only conceptually, both being signified as formal with respect to the person: the essence as its form as subsistent, the property as its form as proper or incommunicable.
claims: Person and essence are really identical in God, since the divine nature subsists by itself without individuating matter.
They differ conceptually: person signifies God as subsistent and proper, essence as simple and common, property as proper and distinguishing.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e172.summary: Reply to the first argument. Begetting and similar acts are attributed to a divine person by the twofold mode of signifying that distinguishes it from the essence: they signify the distinguishing relations, and they signify by way of act, and every act belongs to a subsistent, complete thing. So they cannot be attributed to the essence because they are attributed to the hypostasis, since they belong to the hypostasis in that in which it is not the same as the essence, and the argument commits the fallacy of accident.
claims: Acts belong to the person by its relation and subsistence, not to the essence; the argument is a fallacy of accident.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e175.summary: Reply to the second argument. The same cannot be affirmed and denied of the same as such, but where something is distinguished, affirmations and negations pertaining to that distinction can be true of it, since every distinction, real or conceptual, rests on affirmation and negation, as with synonyms: 'tunica', 'vestis', and 'indumentum' mean the same thing, so things true of the thing cannot be affirmed of one and denied of another, but things true of the names can ('indumentum is neuter, vestis is not'). So since person and essence are really the same, nothing pertaining to the thing can be predicated of the essence and denied of the person (uncreated, God), but what pertains to the concept that distinguishes them can ('the essence is common, the person is not'; 'the person begets, the essence does not').
claims: Predicates of the thing are shared by person and essence; predicates of their distinguishing concepts are not.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e178.summary: Reply to the third argument. Properly nothing in God is under another, so Augustine does not accept 'substance' in God (Dist. 8) and Richard changed 'subsistence' to 'existence', and 'supposit' is not proper there if it refers to the thing. We use such names according to our understanding, which takes in God something corresponding to two things in creatures, one under the other, as a per se existing thing under a simple common form: it takes something simple in God corresponding to form and something subsistent, really the same as the simple, and so calls the subsistent thing the supposit of the simple nature.
claims: 'Supposit' is said of God only by our mode of understanding.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e181.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The common is twofold: common in concept, contracted and determined by adding something proper, as genus by difference and species individuated by matter; and common in reality, which remains undivided and needs no addition, as the essence in the three persons. The concept of person includes a concept, relation, not in the concept of essence, but that relation does not differ really from the essence, so it makes no composition and distinguishes person not from essence but from person.
claims: The essence is common in reality and needs no contracting addition.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e184.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. The three persons are united in the essence, which is wholly the same in reality as each but differs conceptually from each, since 'person' includes relation. Relation, compared to the essence, differs only conceptually, but compared to its opposed correlative makes a real distinction, since relation distinguishes really only by its opposed respect, which is not toward what it is in but toward what it is said of, so it is not really distinct from the essence or person it is in but from the other person it is said toward.
claims: Relation is conceptually distinct from the essence and really distinct from the opposed person.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e196.summary: First argument that it is unfitting to say the three persons are of one essence. Oblique cases are transitive (the grammarians), and transitive construction requires diversity of the things construed, and essence is not diverse from person.
claims: Genitive construction requires diversity.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e199.summary: Second argument, against construing the genitives intransitively ('the gift of the Holy Spirit', i.e. that is the Spirit). As the persons are one essence they are one God, so one could say they are 'of one God', which the text denies.
claims: Intransitive reading would allow 'of one God'.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e202.summary: Third argument. Every oblique construction can be expounded by a preposition with a causal sense, and 'the three persons are from the same essence' or 'through it' is false.
claims: 'Ex eadem essentia' is false.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e206.summary: Fourth argument. 'Thing' and 'one thing' have the same concept (the Philosopher), so if the persons are 'of one essence' they could be said to be 'of essence', which says nothing.
claims: 'Of one essence' reduces to 'of essence'.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e209.summary: Sed contra. As the text says, all Catholics accepted and defended 'homoousion', which means being of one essence.
claims: Homoousion means of one essence.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e212.summary: Thomas's determination. 'The three persons are of one essence' must be granted simply. Not all four causal relations of creatures are found in God. Material causality fits God neither within him nor toward creatures, matter being imperfect and potential. Final causality holds toward creatures, whose end is his goodness, but not within God, since one person is not the end of another, which would imply grades of goodness. Formal causality holds toward creatures, whose exemplar he is, and within God, founded not on a real relation but on the mode of signifying, something being signified as form (essence) and something as subsisting in the form (person). Efficient causality, taken broadly as origin, holds toward creatures and within God, not of the essence to a person but of person to person, founded on a real relation. So every construction within God expresses efficient causality ('the Son of the Father') or formal causality ('the three persons are of one essence'), and these genitives are construed as formal cause.
claims: 'Three persons of one essence' is true, the genitive expressing formal causality by mode of signifying.
In God only formal (conceptual) and broadly efficient (real, origin) causal relations obtain among the persons.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e215.summary: Reply to the first argument. Though essence and person are really the same, they differ conceptually, one signified as form of the other, and that diversity suffices for the grammarian, who considers modes of signifying.
claims: Conceptual diversity suffices for transitive construction.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e218.summary: Reply to the second argument. The construction is not by identity but by relation of form, and since 'God' is not signified as the form of the three persons, they cannot be called 'of one God', which could only be understood possessively; likewise one says 'one essence of three persons'. And 'God' implies the relation of a principle creating and governing.
claims: 'God' is not signified as form, so 'of one God' is not said.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e221.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Ex' and 'de' designate what relates to motion or operation as beginning, not as end, so they designate efficient or material causality, not formal or final, which are rather the end of motion, so the persons are in no way 'from' the same essence; but they can be said to be 'in' the same essence, since 'in' can denote a containing formal cause.
claims: The persons are in one essence, not from it.

ta-l1d34q1-d1e225.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Constructions designating form require two genitives, one signifying the form and the other its determination ('a column of wondrous height'), or one genitive with the force of two ('a man of bloods', i.e. a shedder of much blood). So here one genitive signifies the divine essence and another its simplicity, unity, or some other condition: 'of one essence', 'of the same essence', 'of uncreated essence', but not simply 'of essence'.
claims: Formal genitives need a determining term: 'of one essence', not 'of essence'.

ta-l1d34q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 34 divides Lombard's comparison of person and essence, by identity and by commonness, and his close of the treatise on the Trinity, and announces three questions, the first with articles on whether the essence is the person and whether the three are of one essence.
claims: Person and essence are identical; the essence is common.

ta-l1d34q1-Dd1e135.summary: Article 1 holds that person and essence are really identical in God, since the divine nature subsists by itself without individuating matter, so that by which and what is are the same. They differ conceptually: person signifies God as subsistent and proper, essence as simple and common, property as proper and distinguishing. Acts belong to persons, predicates of the distinguishing concepts are not shared, 'supposit' is said by our mode of understanding, the essence is common in reality without contracting addition, and relation is really distinct only from the opposed person.
claims: Person and essence are really identical, conceptually distinct.
The essence is common in reality; relation distinguishes person from person, not from essence.

ta-l1d34q1-Dd1e188.summary: Article 2 holds that 'three persons of one essence' is true, the genitive expressing formal causality by mode of signifying, since in God only formal (conceptual) and broadly efficient (real, by origin) causal relations obtain within the Godhead. Conceptual diversity suffices for grammar, 'God' is not signified as form, the persons are in one essence but not from it, and the formal genitive needs a determining term.
claims: The persons are of one essence by a genitive of formal cause, and in it, not from it.

ta-l1d34q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 34 compares person and essence. Article 1 holds that they are really identical, the divine nature being self-subsistent without individuating matter, and conceptually distinct as subsistent-proper and simple-common. Article 2 holds that the three persons are of one essence, the genitive expressing a formal causality grounded in the mode of signifying, and that they are in, not from, one essence.
claims: Person and essence are really identical and conceptually distinct.
The three persons are of one essence, by a genitive of formal cause.
